# Bolt Fusion Tech — case studies

Every figure below carries a `shipped` or `target` label. `shipped` means observed
on a running system; `target` means a number we contract to, not one we have
measured. Nothing here is unlabelled.

---

# WarmChats — AI booking for real estate

Live at https://warmchats.com · Write-up: /work/warmchats

## The problem

Real estate leads go cold fast. An agent who replies first usually wins the
appointment, but leads arrive at all hours across email, SMS, Zillow, open houses
and Facebook, and a human cannot be first every time.

## What we built

An always-on follow-up system that is first to every inbound lead.

- **Qualification and routing.** Claude reads each new lead — buyer or seller —
  and routes it, so the reply is appropriate to intent rather than a template.
- **Reply.** GPT-4.1 responds across email and SMS in the agent's voice.
- **Booking.** Confirmed showings write straight to the calendar; no manual step.
- **Tracking.** Every message is recorded, so the agent can see exactly what was
  said on their behalf.

## Architecture

Event-driven microservices: Next.js front end, NestJS and Django services,
PostgreSQL. Each inbound message is an event; qualification, reply generation and
calendar writes are separate consumers, so a failure in one does not silently drop
a lead.

## Numbers

| Value | Label | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `<60s` | First reply to every inbound lead | target |

Source: WarmChats, live in production.

# Intelligent restaurant search — multi-tenant AI retrieval

Write-up: /work/restaurant-search

## The problem

Conversational discovery is easy to demo and expensive to run. A naive
implementation sends every query to a frontier model, so cost scales linearly with
traffic and p95 latency is whatever the model gives you that day. Most AI products
die after launch for exactly this reason — too slow, too expensive, too unstable.

## What we built

Three retrieval lanes, with every query classified *before* any paid inference
runs, so most traffic never reaches a model.

**Keyword lane** — simple intents, no model call.
PostgreSQL ILIKE with PostGIS geo filters. Roughly 80% of traffic, under 80ms.
`$0 marginal cost`

**AI lane** — complex intent becomes structured retrieval.
Claude Haiku parses intent to JSON, then OpenAI embeddings and pgvector cosine
similarity in Postgres. Roughly 20% of traffic, under 1200ms.
`~$0.001 per search`

**Cache lane** — repeat demand disappears at the edge.
Redis, 30-second TTL. The key is tenant plus query plus geo plus filters plus
classification, so two tenants never share a result. Under 15ms.
`30–40% hit rate target`

## Why classification comes first

Routing is deterministic and happens before spend. The expensive path is opt-in,
chosen by the shape of the query rather than by a model deciding whether it wants
to answer. That is what makes the unit economics predictable as volume grows.

## Numbers

| Value | Label | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `<100ms` | Search response, 80% of traffic | shipped |
| `~$0.001` | Average cost per AI query | shipped |
| `~90%` | Of AI calls routed to Haiku, not a frontier model | shipped |

Source: restaurant discovery platform.
